content: 1. Patients should be referred for additional testing to confirm tuberculosis (TB) disease or infection and for further evaluation, following national guidelines. 2. Training and on-the-job capacity building should be conducted for healthcare workers, community health workers, and other service providers to ensure systematic screening for TB symptoms. 3. Regular supportive supervision should be implemented at national, provincial, and district levels to monitor TB screening activities, particularly those performed by community health workers, ensuring adherence to national algorithms and maintaining high-quality screening. 4. Job aids should be developed to outline the steps required to rule out TB disease effectively. 5. Access to chest radiography should be organized through public or private health facilities, mobile vans, or partnerships with private hospitals and radiologists, as per national policy. Free vouchers may also be provided to facilitate access to private services. 6. Standardized tools for data collection should be developed or existing tools updated to include relevant data elements on active case finding (ACF) and activities to rule out TB disease. The national health management information system (HMIS) should summarize data at key steps in the care cascade and report program performance indicators to the national level. 7. Effective TB symptom screening forms the foundation of TB preventive treatment (TPT) services. Additional diagnostic tools, such as tests for TB infection, chest radiography, and rapid diagnostic tests, may be utilized. 8. Key steps in ruling out TB disease and considering TPT include clinical symptom-based screening, such as identifying cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. For children, additional symptoms like poor weight gain, reduced playfulness, or a history of contact with a TB case should be considered. 9. Chest radiography is not mandatory but may be considered for certain groups, such as people living with HIV (PLHIV) on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or asymptomatic close contacts, where resources and capacity allow. 10. Rapid diagnostic tests, such as Xpert MTB/RIF or urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assays, are recommended for TB diagnosis if initial screening tests are positive. 11. Testing for TB infection using tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) is not required for PLHIV or contacts under five years of age. However, in other populations, these tests can help limit unnecessary treatment in low-prevalence settings. 12. Active hepatitis, heavy alcohol consumption, peripheral neuropathy symptoms, concurrent use of hepatotoxic medications, or hypersensitivity to TPT are contraindications for initiating TPT. 13. Counseling should include information on TB infection, the need for TPT, medication adherence, follow-up visits, potential adverse events, and actions to take if TB symptoms or side effects develop. 14. Screening for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women can be integrated into maternal and child health services, immunization clinics, and nutrition programs. 15. TPT and ACF should be integral components of care for PLHIV, particularly in differentiated HIV service delivery models. 16. National programs should convene technical working groups to review strategies for ruling out TB disease before initiating TPT among target populations. 17. Human resource development plans should include hiring, training, mentoring, and sensitization of healthcare workers in TB symptom screening, family counseling, and TPT eligibility evaluation. 18. If chest radiography is used for TB screening, funding should be allocated for equipment, logistics, maintenance, clinician training, and partnerships with private radiography services. 19. Access to rapid TB diagnostics, such as Xpert MTB/RIF and LAM assays, should be expanded. 20. Specimen collection and transportation systems should be strengthened to meet the needs of different target populations, including children. 21. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and job aids for TB symptom screening should be printed and disseminated. 22. Testing for TB infection should not be a mandatory requirement for TPT initiation, especially in high TB incidence settings, as the benefits of treatment outweigh the risks. 23. TST and IGRA should only be used among at-risk groups, such as clinical risk groups, contacts over five years of age, prisoners, and healthcare workers, to identify individuals at high risk for TB infection or disease progression. 24. Governments and donors should invest in building health system capacity for TST and IGRA to avoid unnecessary TPT and related harms while improving acceptance and enabling rapid adoption of new TB infection tests in the future. 25. SOPs should be developed for TST administration, blood specimen collection for IGRA, and interpretation of test results, along with appropriate follow-up mechanisms. 26. Mechanisms should be established to ensure the availability of tuberculin, syringes, and other consumables in the cold chain, as well as to train personnel in TST administration and reading. 27. Laboratory systems should be equipped to conduct IGRA, including phlebotomy, blood specimen processing, incubation, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) reading. 28. Mechanisms for rapid transportation of blood specimens to IGRA testing laboratories should be established, ensuring timely processing within 8–30 hours. 29. National programs may collaborate with non-TB-specific laboratories or private institutions to leverage existing capacity for blood draws and ELISA testing. 30. Testing for TB infection should be targeted to high-risk groups, and results should not be used to assess the efficacy of TPT, as TST and IGRA may remain positive even after successful treatment.
